Speech-to-text transcribes an 11 s clip in 43 ms, 257x real time, whole model
resident, S1–S8 done. **Text-to-speech is 31 ms for 3.25 s of audio**, 105x
real time. T6 is finished: ALBERT 104 ms to 4 (T6a), the F0/N AdaIN stacks 40
to 1 (T6b), the six bidirectional LSTMs 73 to 6 (T6c) and the chain between
them 17 to 8 (T6d) — so **the phoneme side went from 222 ms to 8 and is now
26% of an utterance, over 1.96 ms of GPU time**. The other 74% is the vocoder,
whose 22 ms T4c and T7 cut from 3626.
T8 closed the last open feature: a voice may name a **mixture** of packs, in
upstream's own spelling, and T9 closed the last place where the server cost
more than the model.

**R1 closed the loop and moved the target.** `cmd/roundtrip` runs text through
both endpoints and back — six prose cases return exactly, at **61.6x real
time** — and what it measures is that the two verticals scale in opposite
directions: transcription amortises its fixed cost away to 257x, while
synthesis bottoms out at 8.3 ms per second of audio and then gets **36% worse
per second** by a nineteen-second utterance. `cmd/tts` localises that to
**PL-BERT, 4 ms at 50 tokens and 75 at 321**, which makes the phoneme side 43%
of a paragraph rather than the 26% T6 left it at. See [R1](#r1--the-round-trip-and-what-it-says-to-do-next).

`go run ./cmd/tts -gpu -text 'Hello there.'` speaks, with no Python on the
path. T5 opened with a measurement instead of code — **91% of running-text
tokens are a dictionary lookup and a part-of-speech tagger decides 1.74% of
them** — and ended with the whole of misaki's English G2P ported: five
components exact against their own dumped oracles, twelve measured rules where
spacy's tagger mattered, and a cgo binding to libespeak-ng for the rest.
**The designed corpus is exact, 24 of 24; on 400 sentences nobody chose, 92.4%
of phoneme words agree.** [Write-up](research/t5-kokoro-g2p.md).

content.text:
Done. The loop closes, and the numbers point somewhere specific.

**What I built**

- `cmd/roundtrip` — an HTTP client: text → `POST /v1/audio/speech` → resample → `POST /v1/audio/transcriptions` → text, with the returned text checked against the input (word-level, case/punctuation-insensitive) and a WER when it differs. Nonzero exit on a mismatch. `-reps`, `-csv`, `-text`, `-cases`, `-stress`, `-v`.
- `audio/resample.go` + tests — the round trip needs it: kokoro emits 24 kHz, `backend.STT` refuses anything but 16 kHz (deliberately, so I didn't touch it). Windowed-sinc polyphase; the tests pin the passband against an analytic sine and hold a 10 kHz tone 40+ dB down, which matters because aliased energy would land in parakeet's mel bank as a feature.
- `SPEECH.md` — an R1 section with the measurements, and the status block updated.

**Results** (`go run ./cmd/serve -tts -stt`; six prose cases, 1 word to a paragraph, all exact; two runs at 61.6x and 62.6x real time over 51.6 s of audio):

| | ms/s of audio | share |
|---|---|---|
| speech, server | 10.3 | **63%** |
| transcribe, server | 4.6 | 28% |
| resample, client | 1.4 | 8% |
| http, JSON, multipart, WAV | 0.0 | 0.2% |

Timing is split at the first response byte, and it lands within 1 ms of what the handlers log for `Speak`/`Transcribe` themselves (221 vs 222, 73 vs 74) — so **there is no protocol left to optimise at either endpoint**; it's all model.

**Where to focus.** The per-case rows matter more than the totals, because the two verticals scale in opposite directions:

```
ms per second of audio     1.35s   3.25s   5.05s   8.80s  13.60s  19.52s
speech, server              10.8     8.8     8.3     9.1    10.6    11.3
transcribe, server          11.5     6.6     5.8     4.4     4.1     3.9
```

Parakeet amortises its fixed cost away and ends at 257x. Kokoro bottoms out around 5 s and then gets **36% worse per second of audio** by 19 s — its fit has a *negative* intercept, i.e. it's a curve. `cmd/tts -gpu` localises that: at 50 tokens vs 321, PL-BERT goes 4 ms → 75 ms (**18.8x for 6.4x the tokens**) while the vocoder scales linearly, 21 → 128. So the phoneme side is 43% of a paragraph, not the 26% T6 left it at.

Ranked: (1) PL-BERT's growth with token count — 75 ms of a 225 ms utterance, and superlinear; T6a's 46.6x was measured at the one length where it was cheap. (2) The phoneme side's other 21 ms. (3) A 16 kHz path out of the vocoder — the resample is 8% of the loop, four times what HTTP costs, and pure waste given the consumer. (4) Nothing on parakeet; S10's front end is 48% of *its* pipeline but only 28% of the loop.

Two notes: `-stress` shows the normalisation cases (digits, acronyms) where both models are right and disagree — measured, never counted as failures. And `API.md` still says `-tts-gpu` is off by default; `cmd/serve` has defaulted it to true since T9, so that line is stale — I left it alone as it's outside this change.

message.content: It sounds like text-to-speech is the slowest component, and one part of it doesn't scale linearly?

content.text:
Yes on both, with one caveat on the second.

**TTS is the slower leg**, though both are far faster than real time. Per second of audio produced/consumed: speech 10.3 ms, transcription 4.6 ms — so kokoro costs ~2.2x parakeet and is 63% of the round trip. In real-time terms that's ~87-112x for synthesis against ~180-257x for transcription.

**The non-linear part is PL-BERT.** Same two utterances through `cmd/tts -gpu`, 50 tokens vs 321 (6.4x):

```
bert            4ms  →  75ms    18.8x     superlinear
phoneme side    8ms  →  96ms    12.0x
tail            8ms  →  59ms     7.4x     frames grew 6.0x
vocoder        21ms  → 128ms     6.1x     linear, as it should be
generator      12ms  →  64ms     5.3x
```

Everything downstream of the durations scales with frame count, which is what it's supposed to do. PL-BERT scales with *phoneme tokens*, and 18.8x for 6.4x of them is roughly O(n^1.6) — between linear and quadratic, which is the signature of a quadratic attention term sitting on top of linear GEMMs.

The caveat: 4 ms at 50 tokens is close to this part's dispatch floor for twelve ALBERT layers, so that ratio is measured against a baseline that may be overhead-dominated rather than arithmetic-dominated. That makes the *direction* certain — the endpoint's cost per second of audio provably rises 36% between 5 s and 19.5 s of speech — but not the exponent, and not yet which sub-part inside the twelve layers owns it.

Pinning that is one cheap experiment: sweep `cmd/tts` over five or six token counts and fit, then split bert's own time between attention and the projections. Say the word and I'll run it.

content.text: The sweep settles it — and it's not the GEMM tile, it's attention. Let me correct the R1 write-up with the real numbers:

input.command:
python3 - <<'PY'
p='SPEECH.md'
s=open(p).read()
old = """The vocoder scales with its frames, as it has to. **PL-BERT does not** — 6.4x
the tokens for 18.8x the time — so T6a's 46.6x was measured at the one length
where the phoneme side was cheap, and at paragraph length the phoneme side is
**43% of an utterance rather than 26%**. That is where the next millisecond
on this vertical is, and it displaces "What is left after T7": the excitation
is 1 ms of a 225 ms utterance.

So, in order of what it would buy a round trip:

1. **PL-BERT's growth with token count** — 75 ms of 225, and superlinear, so
   it is worse for every text longer than the one it was tuned on. Twelve
   ALBERT layers over 321 tokens is a shape the GEMM ladder covers; the
   suspects are the attention and a tile chosen at T=50.
2. **The phoneme side's other 21 ms** — the six recurrences are one dispatch
   a timestep (T6c), and a timestep is a phoneme.
3. **A 16 kHz path out of the vocoder.** The client resample is 8.4% of the
   loop and pure waste in a pipeline whose consumer is a 16 kHz model: it is
   four times what HTTP costs. `audio.Resample` is the filter; the question
   is whether the iSTFT head can be asked for the lower rate directly.
4. **Nothing on parakeet.** S10's front end is 48% of *its* pipeline and
   still only 28% of the loop, and it is the leg that already amortises."""

new = """The vocoder scales with its frames, as it has to. **PL-BERT does not** — 6.4x
the tokens for 18.8x the time — so T6a's 46.6x was measured at the one length
where the phoneme side was cheap, and at paragraph length the phoneme side is
**43% of an utterance rather than 26%**. That is where the next millisecond
on this vertical is, and it displaces "What is left after T7": the excitation
is 1 ms of a 225 ms utterance.

### It is the attention, and the kernel says so itself

`TestGPUAlbertScaling` profiles one ALBERT layer per dispatch over six
sequence lengths. Microseconds a layer, on GPU timestamps:

    us a layer           50      100      200      321      410      510
    q / k / v            34/14/9  11/11/11 13/13/13 17/17/17 18/18/18 22/22/21
    attention            44      313     1786     5385     9844    16029
    dense                 9       10       13       17       18       22
    ffn                  14       17       23       34       41       60
    ffn out              22       23       31       39       42       47
    layer               164      412     1915     5560    10039    16266
    12 layers, ms       2.0      4.9     23.0     66.7    120.5    195.2

Every projection is **flat per token** — 17 us at 321 against 14 at 50, which
is a GEMM doing T times one row of work — so the tile is not the problem and
the ladder needs nothing. Attention is **0.87 us a token at 50 and 31.43 at
510**: 364x the time for 10.2x the sequence, which is O(T^2.5) rather than the
O(T²) the arithmetic asks for. It goes from **27% of a layer to 98.5%**.

`shaders/kokoro_bert_attn.comp` documents the decision that became wrong:

> It is deliberately scalar rather than a matrix-core flash kernel, and the
> arithmetic says why: twelve heads over fifty tokens at a head width of 64 is
> **7.7 MFLOP a layer** … A WMMA attention would spend most of its tiles on
> padding — a 50-token sequence is four 16-wide tiles with 14 rows of nothing.

That is sound at fifty tokens and false at three hundred. The extra half-power
above quadratic is in the kernel's shape rather than its work: one workgroup
per (head, query), and its weighted sum runs `if (t < hd)` — **64 of 256 lanes
busy, walking every key serially** — while the score loop re-reads the query
row from global memory once per key. The model's own ceiling is 510 phonemes
(the voice packs have 510 style rows), and there PL-BERT alone is **195 ms**.

So, in order of what it would buy a round trip:

1. **PL-BERT's attention.** 64.6 ms of a 225 ms paragraph and 195 ms at the
   model's ceiling, against 9.6 GFLOP that stage 3c's matrix-core kernel would
   do in a quarter of a millisecond. Two tiers: fixing the scalar kernel's
   occupancy is contained and stays in fp32, and `dit_attention_wmma.comp`
   already takes `HEAD_DIM` as a define, so a 64-wide variant is a build
   rather than a kernel. The gate is not the tensor bound but
   `TestGPUAlbertDurations` — durations are integers and must not move.
2. **The phoneme side's other 21 ms** — the six recurrences are one dispatch
   a timestep (T6c), and a timestep is a phoneme.
3. **A 16 kHz path out of the vocoder.** The client resample is 8.4% of the
   loop and pure waste in a pipeline whose consumer is a 16 kHz model: it is
   four times what HTTP costs. `audio.Resample` is the filter; the question
   is whether the iSTFT head can be asked for the lower rate directly.
4. **Nothing on parakeet.** S10's front end is 48% of *its* pipeline and
   still only 28% of the loop, and it is the leg that already amortises.

**What this does not touch is a short utterance.** At fifty tokens PL-BERT is
2 ms of a 29 ms utterance and attention is 0.5 ms of that, so the whole of
item 1 is worth nothing to "Hello." — it is worth 1.4x on a paragraph and
~2.5x at the ceiling, and it is worth removing a term that gets worse the
longer anyone dictates."""
assert s.count(old)==1
s=s.replace(old,new)
open(p,'w').write(s)
PY
echo ok

cat >> SPEECH.md <<'EOF'

## T10 — PL-BERT's attention on the matrix cores, done

R1 said synthesis got 36% worse per second of audio as an utterance
lengthened, and `TestGPUAlbertScaling` said all of it was one dispatch. The
fix is not a new kernel. `shaders/dit_attention_wmma.comp` is stage 3c's
flash attention and already carries `HEAD_DIM` as a compile-time define, so
ALBERT's 768-over-12 head width is a *build* of it — `-DHEAD_DIM=64
-DQT=1 -DKTIL=4 -DWAVE=32`, with `CAUSAL`, `GQA`, `REL_BIAS` and `OUT_F16`ary
all zero — plus the same build of `dit_pack_f16.comp` to lay q, k and v out as
16x16 fp16 fragment tiles. Two `//go:generate` lines and no new GLSL.

Microseconds per ALBERT layer, per dispatch, on GPU timestamps:

    us a layer          50      100      200      321      410      510
    scalar attention    43      320     1774     5394    10052    15976
    wmma attention       3        6       11       25       29       38
    + three packs        6        6        7       10       12       15
    scalar, layer      161      420     1903     5569    10247    16218
    wmma, layer         81      105      148      206      231      288
    speedup, layer    2.00x    4.01x   12.88x   27.03x   44.44x   56.27x

    PL-BERT, 12 layers, ms
    scalar             1.9      5.0     22.8     66.8    123.0    194.6
    wmma               1.0      1.3      1.8      2.5      2.8      3.5

**The kernel that was quadratic now amortises.** Attention was 0.87 us a token
at fifty and 31.33 at five hundred and ten — 36x the cost per token for 10.2x
the sequence. On the matrix cores it is **0.19 us a token at fifty and 0.10 at
510**, packs included: it gets *cheaper* per token, because a flash kernel's
per-query-tile cost is fixed and the tile is 16 rows whether the utterance
fills it or not. That is also why there is no crossover and no fallback — at
the reference fifty tokens, where the tiles are mostly padding and the three
packs buy nothing, it is still 2.0x faster a layer.

What it cost: 2.4 MB of fp16 arena for three per-head plane sets at the 512
ceiling, and three pack dispatches a layer at 3-5 us each. `ScalarAttn` keeps
the old kernel as the oracle.

### The numerics did not move, and that is the whole gate

fp16 operands with fp32 accumulators is what the matrix cores implement, so
the scores are the exposure. They are also bounded: the running max is folded
in before every exponential and P is at most 1 by construction.

The measurements, none of which changed from the scalar path:

| | |
|---|---|
| Layer by layer against the CPU reference | **4.2e-4** at layer 0 to **2.4e-3** at layer 11, bound 6e-3 |
| The whole encoder, `Apply` | **2.4e-3** — the same figure the scalar kernel gave |
| **Durations** | **0 of 50 differ**; largest unrounded drift **0.0048 frames** |
| The F0 curve the durations feed | 2.6e-4 |

The durations are the one that matters and the reason this stage was safe to
do: they are a sum of sigmoids rounded to integers, they decide the length of
every phoneme, and a single flipped rounding shifts the whole waveform after
it — so no sample-wise comparison downstream would mean anything. 60 kokoro
tests pass, including T3's reference waveform.

### End to end

    "Speech synthesis and speech recognition are ..." (319 phonemes, 19.525 s)

    stage           T9      T10
    bert            75ms    12ms     2.5 ms of it on the device
    phonemes        96ms    33ms     43% of an utterance -> 20%
    generator       64ms    66ms
    tail            59ms    57ms
    vocoder        128ms   129ms     57% -> 80%
    total          225ms   162ms     86.9x -> 120.5x real time

The vocoder is the majority again, which is where T4 left it and where a
fixed-cost-per-frame stage belongs. And the round trip, two runs each:

| | T9 | T10 |
|---|---|---|
| The loop over 51.6 s of audio | 61.6x / 62.6x | **70.1x / 70.1x** |
| Speech leg, ms per second of audio | 10.3 | **8.2** |
| … at 19.5 s specifically | 11.3 | **8.1** |
| Fit against audio length | -10.5 ms + 11.5 ms/s | **+2.7 ms + 7.9 ms/s** |

A negative intercept is a curve pretending to be a line. The intercept is now
positive and small, the slope is flat from five seconds to nineteen, and
`r²` is 0.999 — which is the actual result of this stage: not the 1.4x, but
that there is no longer a length at which synthesis gets worse.
EOF

content.text:
Done — the port is in, validated, and measured.

**What I was offering, plainly:** PL-BERT is a small transformer kokoro runs over the phonemes *before* any audio exists, to decide how long each sound should last. Its attention step was written as a simple kernel back when utterances were ~50 phonemes, and the cost of that kernel grows with the square of the phoneme count. At paragraph length it had become 98% of the work. The offer was to move it onto the matrix-core (WMMA) attention kernel this repo already has for four other models — and it turned out to be a *build* of that kernel at ALBERT's head width (`-DHEAD_DIM=64`), not new code: two `//go:generate` lines, three pack dispatches per layer, and ~110 lines of wiring.

**Throughput, measured**

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| One ALBERT layer at 510 phonemes (the model's ceiling) | 16.2 ms | **288 µs** (56x) |
| PL-BERT, all 12 layers, at a 321-phoneme paragraph | 66.8 ms | **2.5 ms** |
| A 19.5 s utterance, end to end | 225 ms (86.9x real time) | **162 ms (120.5x)** |
| The round trip over 51.6 s of audio | 61.6x / 62.6x | **70.1x / 70.1x** |
| Speech leg per second of audio, at 19.5 s | 11.3 ms | **8.1 ms** |

The headline isn't the 1.4x. It's that **the curve became a line**: the speech leg used to fit as −10.5 ms + 11.5 ms/s (a negative intercept means it accelerates away from you), and now fits +2.7 ms + 7.9 ms/s at r²=0.999, flat from 5 seconds out to 19.5. There is no longer a length at which synthesis gets worse per second. As predicted, short utterances didn't move — "Hello." is 31 ms before and after — and even at the 50-phoneme reference length the new kernel is 2.0x faster per layer, so there's no crossover and no fallback needed.

**Quality, gated not assumed.** Attention operands are now fp16 (that's what the matrix cores implement), so the risk was real and the repo already had the right gate: durations are integers, and one flipped rounding would shift the whole waveform after it.

- Layer-by-layer against the CPU reference: 4.2e-4 → 2.4e-3 at layer 11, bound 6e-3
- Whole encoder: **2.4e-3 — the identical figure the old kernel gave**
- **Durations: 0 of 50 differ**, largest unrounded drift 0.0048 frames
- F0 curve 2.6e-4; all 60 kokoro tests pass, including T3's reference waveform

**Also in this change:** `TestGPUAlbertScaling` now profiles both kernels side by side and asserts the *shape* of each — the old one must still be superlinear (it's the oracle), the new one must not be, and no projection may grow per token. That's what stops this regressing quietly. Write-ups are in SPEECH.md (T10) and TTS.md.

Two things I found and did not fix, both now item 2 and 3 on R1's list: with attention gone, `bert` is 12 ms of that paragraph and **only 2.5 ms of it is on the GPU** — the rest is the host-side embedding stack, whose code comment says it's "not worth a dispatch" and was written at fifty rows, the same stale assumption in the same file. And the client-side 24→16 kHz resample is now 9.7% of the loop, thirty times what HTTP costs.
